[2023](#page-23-13)). The aim is to better understand the temporal evolution of freezeup and breakup cycles through detailed ice concentration observations. Monthly median ice concentration values, retrieved from daily VIIRS observations, are presented in Fig. [10](#page-17-0). These results highlight notable spatial variations in ice concentration across the NERFC, with higher concentrations observed in northern rivers such as the Black, Salmon, Moose, Saint John, and Aroostook Rivers. In contrast, lower ice concentrations were noted in southern rivers such as the Hudson and Housatonic Rivers. During December, median ice concentrations varied between 2% and 40% with a standard deviation of 7.2%. This variation continued into January, where concentrations ranged from 6 to 47% with a standard deviation of 7.7%, and into February, with concentrations ranging from 4 to 59% and a standard deviation of 10.2%. By March, ice concentrations ranged from 4 to 62% with a standard deviation of 12.5%. Notable increases in ice concentration began in December, particularly in northern regions of the NERFC such as the Saint John, Androscoggin, Aroostook, Allagash, and Black Rivers, as well as in western parts such as the upper Mohawk and Salmon Rivers, where median values ranged between 30% and 40%. Southern parts, such as the lower Hudson River, exhibited concentrations below 10%. In January, an increase in ice concentrations across the NERFC was observed, with upstream areas of the Hudson and Connecticut Rivers surpassing 20%. February maintained or increased these concentrations, especially in northern rivers like Saint John, where some reaches showed values above 50%. By March, a marked decrease in ice concentration was noted in southern rivers such as the Hudson, Connecticut, Mohawk, Pomperaug, and Housatonic Rivers, while northern rivers like the Aroostook, Saint John, Allagash, Mattawamkeag, Penobscot, and Piscataquis maintained higher concentrations, with an overall median value of 38%. To further capture the variance in ice development, the difference in median ice concentration between February and December was computed. This analysis highlights the evolution from initial ice formation to stable ice cover across most rivers by February, as depicted in Fig. [11.](#page-18-0) The selected time frame specifically aims to encapsulate the maturation of ice cover, serving as a proxy for ice cover growth. In southern regions, such as the Hudson River, minimal changes in ice concentration were observed, with differences typically under 5%. In contrast, northern rivers exhibited notable increases. The Aroostook and Saint John Rivers, for example, showed increases ranging from 5 to 20%, with more pronounced increments observed in downstream areas. This pattern demonstrates the typical downstream-to-upstream progression of ice formation in these regions. Coastal rivers, affected by tidal effects and anthropogenic activities such as flow regulation and ice breaking, displayed minor variations in ice concentration, generally between 5 and 10%. However, exceptions like the Kennebec and Androscoggin Rivers, which are situated at higher latitudes, experienced increases of up to 20%. Additionally, in non-tidal tributaries such as the Sacandaga River, a primary tributary of the Hudson River, ice concentration values increased by 20 to 30%. These findings provide an overview of the changes in ice conditions from freeze-up to stable ice cover across the NERFC domain. The observed variability underscores that the growth and progression of ice formation during the cold season are predominantly influenced by latitude, illustrating the importance of geographical location and climatological factors in river ice dynamics.

# **4 Discussion** In this study, we leveraged in-situ observations and remote sensing data to investigate river ice phenology and climatology in the Northeast United States. By integrating groundbased measurements with satellite-derived river ice data from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite, we identified the temporal and spatial patterns of ice formation and breakup dates across the Northeast River Forecast Center domain. Our findings revealed that ice formation in northern rivers typically commences from mid-November to mid-December, indicative of the influence of regional hydroclimatic conditions, which controls earlier freeze-ups due to lower temperatures at higher latitudes. Furthermore, breakup dates in the NERFC were observed to span from mid-February to mid-April, with predominant open water conditions occurring in lower latitudes and delayed transitions to open water conditions in higher latitudes. These observations align with the general patterns noted in previous studies, such as those by Hodgkins et al. ([2005\)](#page-23-19) and Newton and Mullan [\(2021](#page-23-4)), which investigated freeze-up and breakup timing in specific rivers and lakes located in the northeastern parts of the United Stated. Discrepancies noted between in-situ and VIIRS data underscored the sensitivity of remote sensing to early ice formation, particularly in detecting border ice, frazil ice, and ice floes. This sensitivity contrasts with in-situ measurements, which primarily capture ice-affected flow. Such contrasts highlight the imperative for a synergistic approach, integrating both ![](_page_16_Picture_13.jpeg) M. Abdelkader et al. **60** Page 18 of 24 ![](_page_17_Figure_1.jpeg) **Fig. 10** Temporal and spatial variations in median ice concentration from VIIRS observations during (**a**) December, (**b**) January, (**c**) February, and (**d**) March. Monthly variation of median ice concentration values as a function of river's reaches (**e**) ![](_page_17_Picture_3.jpeg) ![](_page_18_Figure_3.jpeg) **Fig. 11** Spatial variations in the difference between median ice concentration in february and december ground-based observations with remote sensing retrievals. However, we must acknowledge that differences in the coverage periods of in-situ and VIIRS observations may also contribute to discrepancies in the calculated median freeze up and breakup dates. Detecting breakup dates accurately from in-situ observations poses considerable challenges due to the subjectivity and lack of a clear unified methodological framework for how measurements are flagged in the presence of ice. While we have carefully investigated the data used in this study, assuming the reliability of these flags, a more robust and systematic approach is required to enable a continental-scale assessment. The subjectivity and timing of measurement flags often introduce discrepancies in accurately capturing ice formation and breakup events, necessitating innovative methods to refine site-based observations of ice conditions. A comprehensive database, similar to the Canadian River Ice Database (de Rham et al. [2020](#page-22-16)), created based on in-situ measurements, would advance the regional and continentalscale assessment of river ice phenology across the United States. Additionally, utilizing camera footage in conjunction with flow data could yield more precise ice presence flags, enhancing the reliability of ice detection (Ansari et al. [2017](#page-22-17)). Furthermore, the adoption of autonomous systems for ice monitoring, as explored by Aslamov et al. ([2021\)](#page-22-18), along with remote data collection techniques on ice breakup dynamics, as demonstrated by Beltaos et al. [\(2011\)](#page-22-19), underscores the potential for significant improvements in in-situ measurements. By improving the accuracy of in-situ measurements through these advanced technological solutions, researchers and policymakers can gain a deeper understanding of ice phenology, contributing to more effective and timely decisions in hydrological and climatological applications. In this study, remote sensing of river ice was performed based on retrieval from VIIRS observations. While VIIRS offers superior spatial resolution compared to Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), its data coverage spans only 12 years. This limited timeframe poses significant challenges for conducting long-term trend analysis, which is vital for understanding the broader impacts of climate variability on river ice dynamics. To potentially extend the analysis period and thus enable more comprehensive climatological studies, MODIS data could be utilized, offering up to 22 years of observations. However, the utility of MODIS is somewhat diminished by its thermal band's coarser spatial resolution of 1 km, which may not adequately capture detailed ice formations in riverine environments, particularly for smaller or narrower rivers (Chaouch et al. [2014](#page-22-13)). In this context, VIIRS remains a more suitable alternative due to its finer spatial resolution of 370 m within the thermal band, which is critical for accurately detecting and mapping river ice (Temimi et al. [2023\)](#page-23-13). Therefore, while extending the temporal scope through the inclusion of MODIS data could provide valuable additional insights into longer-term trends, the resolution constraints must be carefully considered. The optimal integration of these satellite technologies, each with its strengths and limitations, provides an opportunity for advancing our understanding of the ![](_page_18_Picture_10.jpeg) temporal evolution of river ice phenology and informs the development of more robust predictive models for hydrological and climatological applications. The trend analysis conducted in this study using the MMK revealed no statistically significant changes in freeze-up or breakup dates over the period from 1985 to 2023. This suggests that definitive conclusions regarding major alterations in the freeze-up and breakup cycles within the Northeast River Forecast Center regions cannot be conclusively established. However, the trend magnitude test results showed tendency toward later freeze-up dates across the NERFC regions which could be influenced by several climatological factors. Notably, it is suggested that rising autumn and early winter temperatures could explain the tendency towards later ice formations. Concurrently, it is indicated that declining snow cover rates impact the thermal regimes near the surface and ground, which in turn affects the timing of ice formation. This warming trend, coupled with decreasing rates in snow area coverage, could potentially influence ice formation dates, although these changes have not shown statistical significance in ice phenology series. Further, climatological studies in our study area have documented that increases in precipitation, particularly during the tropical storm periods from June to November, contribute substantially to the region's total precipitation (Hawcroft et al. [2012](#page-23-20); Kunkel et al. [2013](#page-23-21); Agel et al. [2015](#page-22-20)). Such increases in precipitation are shown to elevate river and lake discharge levels, complicating the stabilization and subsequent freezing of water surfaces. While the trend analysis did not yield statistically significant changes, the interplay of these climatological factors is suggested to indicate a complex relationship between atmospheric conditions and the onset of river ice formation. Although this study did not analyze the influence of human intervention on river ice dynamics, it is acknowledged that regions like the Northeast United States are significantly affected by anthropogenic activities influencing the river ice regime (Miara et al. [2013](#page-23-11); Zhang et al. [2023](#page-23-22)). The effects of river regulation, dams and reservoirs, and thermal pollution (warmer water from industrial cooling or wastewater enters the river) also play critical roles in shaping river ice dynamics (Fukś [2023](#page-22-0); Takács et al. [2013](#page-23-23)). Results obtained in this study align with previous research on specific rivers in the region. For instance, in the Saint John River, located in the northern part of the NERFC, December temperatures near the study site suggest a slight warming trend since 1949. However, this change was not statistically significant (Burrell and Beltaos [2022](#page-22-23); Newton et al. [2024\)](#page-23-24). On the other hand, earlier freeze-up dates with a magnitude of 0.2 days/year were reported. In these studies, which included data from 1950 to 2020, it was discussed that earlier ice-cover formation is promoted by lower discharges. Newton and Mullan ([2021\)](#page-23-4) reported a predominance of change toward later freeze-up dates over northeastern parts of the United States for the period between 1976 and 2005, with a rate ranging between 0 and 8 days per decade, with most of the studied sites showing non-significant trends. The comparison with previous studies highlights the impact of time series length on the obtained trend results; however, there is an indication that the tendency towards later freeze-up conditions is emerging, underscoring the need to continue monitoring and investigating changes in river phenology variability.

The observed tendency towards earlier breakup dates in the NERFC can be attributed to a strong correlation between temperature increases and ice phenology patterns in North American rivers, as detailed by Newton and Mullan [\(2021](#page-23-4)). Specifically, for the Northeast US, the period from February to April is crucial, with rising air temperatures being recognized as facilitating thermal ice breakup. Additionally, it is noted that precipitation significantly influences breakup dynamics, contributing to increased peak breakup flows through the melting process (Prowse [2005](#page-23-2); Beltaos [2007](#page-22-12)). Studies on precipitation climatology emphasize the impact of extreme precipitation events and the number of rainy days during these months in both coastal and inland Northeast regions (Hawcroft et al. [2012](#page-23-20); Agel et al. [2015\)](#page-22-20). Notably, the intensity of precipitation in coastal areas is reported to be higher than in inland regions (Agel et al. [2015\)](#page-22-20), which aligns with the earlier breakup dates observed in coastal sites within this study. Precipitation and extreme weather events in the Northeast United States, including both inland and coastal regions, are presented as posing a significant challenge to river ice dynamics. In the northern parts of the NERFC, warming trends are shown to dominate, with a tendency for earlier breakup dates being observed. It has been shown in previous studies that in North America, warming trends for the number of annual open-water days were initially driven by earlier breakup dates, which were then further increased by later freeze-up dates (Newton and Mullan [2021](#page-23-4); Futter [2003;](#page-22-21) Brammer et al. [2015](#page-22-22)).

The temporal trends of breakup dates identified in our study are consistent with findings from earlier research, demonstrating some overlap in the periods analyzed. For example, Newton and Mullan ([2021\)](#page-23-4) examined ice breakup dates in this region across various intervals, noting that from 1931 to 1960 and 1979–2005, the trends were not statistically significant. These findings align with our observations from 1985 to 2023, where trends toward earlier breakup dates were noted; however, these results were not statistically significant based on the Mann-Kendall test (see Fig. [4](#page-9-0) in Newton and Mullan [\(2021](#page-23-4)). Interestingly, Newton and Mullan's analysis identified significant trends within the periods between 1946 and 1975 and 1961–1990. During

![](_page_19_Picture_8.jpeg)

these times, later breakup dates in the earlier interval and earlier breakups in the later interval were documented. This fluctuation in trends underscores the variability in climatic influences over different decades. The last segment of their study, spanning from 1976 to 2005, parallels our study period and further corroborates the continuation of these trends, albeit without statistical significance.

In this study, the correlation analysis between ice phenology series and climate oscillation series revealed significant links between the North Atlantic Oscillation and freeze-up series, as well as the El Niño-Southern Oscillation and breakup series. These findings are aligned with those reported by Newton and Mullan ([2021\)](#page-23-4), where similar influences on North American rivers and lakes' ice phenology were observed. The observed correlations with NAO and NAOJ, although not as strong, highlight the interplay between atmospheric conditions and river freeze-up processes. It is indicated that positive phases of NAO, associated with milder and drier winters, tend to delay the onset of freeze-up, whereas negative phases, linked to colder and wetter conditions, are seen to accelerate this process.

Moreover, it is noted that a stronger positive NAO phase results in an increase in stronger westerly winds, drawing warmer air across northern Europe fed from the North Atlantic Drift and the Norwegian Current (Hurrell [1995](#page-23-28)). This relationship is influenced not only by temperature but also by other atmospheric and hydrological factors such as precipitation patterns, wind speed, and solar radiation, alongside antecedent conditions like water temperature and river flow. These elements interact in a multifaceted manner, influencing the heat exchange between the atmosphere and the river system, thus affecting the timing and extent of ice formation. These factors collectively affect the heat exchange between the atmosphere and the river system, thus impacting the timing and extent of ice formation. Additionally, studies such as those by Notaro et al. ([2013\)](#page-23-29) have shown that lake-effect snowfall in the Northeast U.S. is associated with negative NAO patterns, further illustrating the multifaceted nature of these interactions.

For river ice breakup, it is suggested by our results that further investigation into the relationships between ice cover durations and smaller-scale synoptic systems is needed to gain more detailed insights. Particularly, the influence of La Niña conditions, which favor the development of nor'easters, is noted to significantly affect temperature and precipitation patterns in eastern North America, as indicated by Bonsal et al. ([2006\)](#page-22-6) and Newton and Mullan [\(2021](#page-23-4)). Specifically, it is observed that La Niña is associated with delayed breakup dates, whereas El Niño conditions are potentially linked to earlier breakups. During El Niño winters, warmer-than-average temperatures are often experienced in the Northeast due to the polar jet stream remaining farther north, which is suggested to reduce the frequency of cold air outbreaks, potentially explaining the earlier breakup dates. Further, Kim et al. [\(2021](#page-23-25)) highlight that changes in the Tropical–Northern Hemisphere (TNH) atmospheric patterns hold a statistically significant correlation with local surface temperatures in the northeastern United States. Moreover, variation in the TNH pattern in response to the warm phase of ENSO circulation contributes to wintertime hydroclimatic variability in the region, with extreme warm episodes during the winter and spring inducing changes in the flow regime (Kim et al. [2021\)](#page-23-25).

Moreover, the breakup response to the Southern Oscillation Index is influenced by the teleconnection's impact on winter precipitation, which is reported to be below normal during negative SOI phases and above normal during positive phases over the Northeast (Shabbar et al. [1997](#page-23-26)). Weaker La Niña events are indicated to be snowier over the Northeast on average. However, it is emphasized that a substantial portion of variance is not explained by the SOI index alone, as breakup is governed by a complex set of physical and climatological factors other than air temperature. These include winter precipitation and cloud cover influencing the energy balance characterizing the melt period leading up to the event. It is shown that changes in surface albedo and the effectiveness of insolation in reducing ice strength are inherent impacts affecting the breakup timing. Finally in this study the correlation between ice phenology series and climate indices was limited to linear methods. Future research may explore the teleconnection between river ice dynamics and global climate oscillations through advanced methodologies like wavelet analysis, which allows for the examination of variability in both time and frequency domains (Yerdelen and Abdelkader [2021\)](#page-23-27). This approach could uncover non-linear relationships between ice phenology series and climate indices.

Within the context of river ice dynamics in the NERFC domain, breakup jams, predominantly observed from December to April, are recognized as posing significant challenges. These mid-winter breakup jams, driven primarily by rapid temperature fluctuations and heavy precipitation, are complicated in their predictability and the development of effective response strategies. The abrupt nature of these events underscores the ongoing need for focused research to improve predictive modeling and mitigate the impacts of these dynamic phenomena. Moreover, abrupt transitions in large-scale atmospheric flow patterns are observed to trigger extremes in precipitation and temperature that can accelerate snowmelt and increase streamflow within a watershed, contributing to ice jam formation. These rapid changes in environmental conditions are noted to disrupt the stability of ice covers, increasing the likelihood of ice jams.

![](_page_20_Picture_10.jpeg)

For instance, the significant mid-winter breakup observed in 1996 was attributed to a critical regime shift in January of that year. This transition was associated with the enhanced poleward transport of warm, humid air in the warm sector of mid-latitude cyclones over eastern North America. It has been reported by Leathers et al. [\(1998](#page-23-31)) that this atmospheric pattern produced 72-hour precipitation totals ranging from 30 to 90 mm and melted snow water equivalent of 7 to 15 cm. These conditions were found to precipitate ice jams and flooding across several regions in the northeast United States, illustrating the complex interplay between atmospheric conditions and river ice processes (Leathers et al. [1998](#page-23-31)).

Furthermore, the occurrence of mid-winter breakups has been attributed to enhanced moisture transport characteristic of atmospheric rivers. Two different processes are identified in association with these events: a long melting period with low precipitation resulting in extensive snowmelt, followed by short-duration atmospheric rivers producing rain on snow and significantly increasing flow; and a short melting period with high precipitation, where snowmelt occurred primarily during a more intense and long-duration atmospheric river producing heavy precipitation. A previous study have shown that during 1981–2019, in a localized study focusing on a river in Central New Hampshire, 19 of 20 events were preceded by environments characterized by atmospheric rivers along the U.S. East Coast, making synoptic-scale antecedent meteorological characteristics one of the main drivers of mid-winter breakups (Sanders et al. [2020](#page-23-32)).

There remains substantial scope to further investigate the onset of mid-winter breakups within the NERFC. Future studies could benefit from a differentiated approach that examines inland and coastal locations separately. Coastal areas, for instance, may experience weakening in ice cover influenced by tidal effects, adding another layer of complexity to ice dynamics in these regions. Such differentiation is crucial as it can highlight unique hydroclimatic controls and ice behavior that are specific to coastal versus inland river systems. Moreover, the hydroclimatic controls of mid-winter breakup demand a deeper investigation. Developing and accessing variability in ice thickness throughout the seasons could provide valuable climatological insights and support operational decision-making. This approach would not only enhance our understanding of ice phenology but also improve the accuracy of predictive hydrological models.

Building on this, there is an opportunity to deepen the analysis by investigating river ice processes in rivers under the influence of tidal effects. Recent studies in oceanic environments have demonstrated that tides can significantly enhance the kinetic energy of the time-varying flow in contact with ice shelves, thereby increasing melt rates (Hausmann et al. [2020;](#page-23-30) Fromm et al. [2023\)](#page-22-24). However, the impact of tides on the onset of freeze-up and breakup of river ice remains poorly understood. Investigating the interaction of extreme tides with winter ice, especially during mid-winter breakups, could provide valuable insights into how tidal forces influence river ice dynamics. This area of research is crucial for comprehensively understanding the environmental and climatic factors that govern river ice phenology, particularly in estuarine and coastal river systems where tidal influences are pronounced. To effectively investigate these tidal interactions with river ice, it is imperative to utilize high temporal and spatial resolution satellite imagery, augmented by ground observations including time-lapse footage of rivers to capture the dynamic ice movements.

# **5 Conclusions**

In conclusion, this study has effectively utilized remote sensing observations alongside in-situ data to delineate river ice climatology across the Northeast United States. It was observed that ice formation initiates earlier in northern rivers of the NERFC, typically from mid to late November, and later in southern rivers, around mid to late January. Correspondingly, ice breakup patterns are earlier in southern rivers, occurring from late February to early March, and later in northern rivers, extending to mid-April. This results in a longer duration of ice cover from south to north across the region. Spatial and temporal analyses conducted within this study indicate a tendency towards later freeze-up dates across most sites and a general trend towards earlier breakup dates, though both trends remain statistically insignificant. This inconclusiveness highlights the complexity of drawing definitive conclusions about reductions in the period of ice cover based solely on the current dataset and period of study. Furthermore, the study explored the influence of climate oscillations on river ice phenology. It was found that positive phases of the North Atlantic Oscillation typically delay freeze-up dates, whereas their negative phases tend to accelerate these dates. Additionally, El Niño-Southern Oscillation patterns during autumn and winter significantly affect breakup dynamics, with La Niña conditions delaying breakup dates and El Niño conditions facilitating earlier breakups.

A considerable increasing trend was identified in the frequency of mid-winter breakup ice jams, with significant shifts in ice jam frequency patterns noted in 1992 for mid-winter events and 1988 for total events. These findings underscore the dynamic and responsive nature of river ice to climatological changes and signal the need for continued monitoring and research to enhance predictive modeling and management strategies for river ice phenomena. The

![](_page_21_Picture_9.jpeg)

results of this study provide insights for the development of hydrological monitoring approaches in cold regions and informed decision-making in water resource management and ice induced hazard mitigation.

### **Key Points:**

- Flood maps derived from Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) are subject to nearest flowpath limitations that affect inundation skill
- A means of resolving this limitation is provided by reducing HAND processing units to level paths with effective unit stream order
- Discretizing the stream network for HAND computation affects the stage-discharge relationship and leads to higher skill inundation

text:
# **Extending Height Above Nearest Drainage to Model Multiple Fluvial Sources in Flood Inundation Mapping Applications for the U.S. National Water Model**

**Fernando Aristizabal1,2,3 [,](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-2525-4712) Fernando Salas3 , [Greg](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8323-5339)ory Petrochenkov1,3 [,](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9247-821X) Trevor Grout1,3,4, Brian Avant1,3, [Bra](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9849-7411)dford Bates1,3, Ryan Spies1,3 , Nick Chadwick<sup>3</sup> , Zachary Wills1,3, and Jasmeet Judge<sup>2</sup>**

Lynker, Leesburg, VA, USA, 2 Center for Remote Sensing, Agricultural and Biological Engineering Department, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL, USA, 3 National Water Center, Office of Water Prediction, National Weather Service, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, Tuscaloosa, AL, USA, 4 Colorado Basin River Forecast Center, National Weather Service, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, Salt Lake City, UT, USA

**Abstract** Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND), a drainage normalizing terrain index, is a means able of producing flood inundation maps (FIMs) from the National Water Model (NWM) at large scales and high resolutions using reach-averaged synthetic rating curves. We highlight here that HAND is limited to producing inundation only when sourced from its nearest flowpath, thus lacks the ability to source inundation from multiple fluvial sources. A version of HAND, known as Generalized Mainstems (GMS), is proposed that discretizes a target stream network into segments of unit Horton-Strahler stream order known as level paths (LPs). The FIMs associated with each independent LP are then mosaiced together, effectively turning the stream network into discrete groups of homogeneous unit stream order by removing the influence of neighboring tributaries. Improvement in mapping skill is observed by significantly reducing false negatives at river junctions when the inundation extents are compared to FIMs from that of benchmarks. A more marginal reduction in the false alarm rate is also observed due to a shift introduced in the stage-discharge relationship by increasing the size of the catchments. We observe that the improvement of this method applied at 4%–5% of the entire stream network to 100% of the network is about the same magnitude improvement as going from no drainage order reduction to 4%–5% of the network. This novel contribution is framed in a new open-source implementation that utilizes the latest combination of hydro-conditioning techniques to enforce drainage and counter limitations in the input data.

**Plain Language Summary** Flooding is one of the most impactful natural disasters on life and property. The United States National Water Model (NWM) provides flood forecasts to adequately warn people for safe evacuations and protective measures across the entire country. To convert streamflow from the NWM to flood inundation maps (FIM), a model, Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND), is used that translates elevation data from height above mean sea-level to height above the nearest river. This model suffers from issues in mapping performance because inundation sourced from rivers is only considered from the nearest river. We developed a technique that mitigates these errors by removing consideration for neighboring tributaries in the relative elevation computation process. This is done by splitting the stream network into continuous river segments known as level paths (LPs) which removes the effects of tributaries. HAND is computed independently for each LP and the resulting FIMs are mosaiced together to form one seamless map. By computing HAND and catchments on an LP scale, catchments and FIMs are allowed to overlap which can account for multiple river sources of inundation especially at river confluences. We compared these HAND derived FIMs to maps from physically-based models and found improvement in mapping performance.

### **1. Introduction**

Flooding is one of the most significant natural disasters in the United States (US) affecting both the loss of life and property. In 2017 and 2019, river and flash flooding combined represented the leading cause of death and the second leading cause in 2018 among all natural disasters in the US (National Weather Service, [2018](#page-29-0), [2019](#page-29-1); Service, [2020b\)](#page-30-0). More than an average of 104 deaths per year are attributed to flood events from the 10 year period ending in 2019 (Service, [2020a\)](#page-30-1). With respect to property damages, river and flash flooding have contributed to 60.7, 1.6, and 3.7 billion non-inflation adjusted US dollars in the annual periods of 2017–2019, respectively

**Validation:** Fernando Salas, Trevor Grout, Brian Avant, Bradford Bates, Ryan Spies

**Writing – review & editing:** Fernando Salas, Gregory Petrochenkov, Trevor Grout, Brian Avant, Bradford Bates, Ryan Spies, Jasmeet Judge

(National Weather Service, [2018,](#page-29-0) [2019](#page-29-1); Service, [2020b\)](#page-30-0), with the large spike in 2017 attributed to the Hurricane Harvey event along the Gulf Coast. Trends related to flood damages and fatalities have been steadily increasing over recent decades (Corringham & Cayan, [2019;](#page-27-0) Downton et al., [2005;](#page-27-1) Kunkel et al., [1999](#page-28-0); Mallakpour & Villarini, [2015](#page-28-1); Pielke Jr. & Downton, [2000](#page-29-2)). Some are expecting that the hydrologic cycle will intensify due to climate change which will lead to more extreme precipitation in some areas along with a greater risk of flooding (Milly et al., [2002;](#page-29-3) Tabari, [2020;](#page-30-2) Wing et al., [2018](#page-30-3)). Increasing trends in frequency and risk are not uniform across spatial regions with work by Slater and Villarini [\(2016](#page-30-4)) indicating that trends are increasing across the US Midwest and Great Lakes regions while decreasing in the coastal Southeast, Southwest, and California.

### **1.1. Operational Forecasting**

Operational flood forecasting systems are primary tools in developing accurate forecasts for public awareness prior to life threatening and property damaging events. One of these operational systems is the Advanced Hydrologic Prediction System (AHPS) maintained by the National Oceanic Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Weather Service (NWS) with thousands of forecasting points across the US at typically short forecast horizons of 24 or 72 hr (McEnery et al., [2005\)](#page-29-4). AHPS utilizes a variety of techniques including distributed modeling (Duan, [2003;](#page-27-2) Koren et al., [2004](#page-28-2); Reed et al., [2004\)](#page-29-5), ensemble forecasting (Day, [1985](#page-27-3); Herr et al., [2002;](#page-28-3) Mullusky et al., [2002](#page-29-6); Seo et al., [2000](#page-29-7)), hydraulic routing (Cajina et al., [2002;](#page-27-4) Fread, [1973](#page-28-4)), multi-sensor precipitation methods (Bonnin, [1996;](#page-27-5) Breidenbach et al., [1999;](#page-27-6) Kondragunta, [2001](#page-28-5); Seo & Breidenbach, [2002](#page-29-8)), flood inundation mapping (Cajina et al., [2002\)](#page-27-4), and calibration techniques (Duan, [2003](#page-27-2); Gupta et al., [2003;](#page-28-6) Hogue et al., [2003;](#page-28-7) Parada et al., [2003;](#page-29-9) Z. Zhang, [2003\)](#page-30-5). AHPS provides forecasting services in the form of ensemble streamflows at more than 3,600 locations and flood inundation maps (FIM) at more than 150 of those points shown in Figure [1](#page-2-0). Additionally, two forecasting networks, Full Resolution (FR) and Mainstems (MS) stream networks, relevant to the National Water Model (NWM) (see Section [1.2](#page-1-0)) are rendered in Figure [1.](#page-2-0) The FR network refers to the entire NWM forecasting domain while MS refers to the subset of the FR network that is at or downstream of AHPS forecasting points (see Section [1.2](#page-1-0)). On an approximate basis, there is only one forecast point every 1,450 km of river (FR) and one forecast point with FIM every 29,000 km of river (FR). Despite the AHPS advances in operational flood forecasting, it lacks sufficient domain coverage, spatial resolution, and long-range forecast horizons to address the increasingly complex water challenges facing the US.

### **1.2. National Water Model** Additional work is required to address the gaps that the AHPS leaves in terms of spatial resolution, spatial coverage, and temporal forecast horizons. In response to growing stakeholder demand for enhanced and integrated water resource forecasts, the Office of Water Prediction (OWP) at the National Water Center (NWC) along with its partners at the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) have developed and implemented operationally the NWM which is a configuration of the Weather Research and Forecasting Hydrologic Model (WRF-Hydro) (Cosgrove et al., [2019](#page-27-7); Gochis et al., [2021](#page-28-8); Salas et al., [2018\)](#page-29-10). The NWM forecasts river discharges at more than 2.7 million forecast points at a variety of time horizons including lookback-range (3–28 hr), short-range (18 hr), medium-range (10 days) and long-range (30 days) forecast horizons. The NWM enhances the spatial and temporal domain of the current AHPS capabilities operated at the 13 River Forecast Centers (RFC) in areas known as "hydro-blind." As a complement to the operational NWM, RFC forecasts from AHPS forecast points are assimilated in the NWM and routed downstream to the next downstream AHPS forecast point where the process iterates again. This assimilation into the NWM is used to enhance forecasting skill by leveraging best available regional-scale forecasts. The river network upon which this special assimilation technique operates on is herein referred to as the Mainstem (MS) stream network. Figure [1](#page-2-0) shows the NWM V2.1 FR stream network as well as the NWM V2.1 MS network. The MS network contains roughly 120 thousand forecasting points or roughly 4.4% of the reaches of the FR stream network. The National Hydrography Data set Plus (NHDPlus) V2.1 is the basis for the "hydrofabric" in the NWM due to its comprehensive use with the hydrologic communities' stakeholders (McKay et al., [2012;](#page-29-11) NHDPlusHR GDB, [2021](#page-29-12)). The term "hydrofabric" is used within the NWM jargon to describe the subset of hydrography composed of the geospatial data sets required for hydrologic modeling including but not limited to stream networks, catchments, channel properties, and elevation data. The NWM provides stream forecasts at these hydrofabric segments using the Muskingum-Cunge method to reduce computational requirements of a continental scale ARISTIZABAL ET AL. 2 of 31 ![](_page_2_Figure_3.jpeg) **Figure 1.** Forecast points with and without Flood Inundation Maps (FIM) in United States' Advanced Hydrologic Prediction System (AHPS). Note that only a small fraction of the AHPS forecast points have existing FIM. Also shown are the National Water Model (NWM) stream networks at the Full Resolution (FR) and Mainstems (MS) resolution. The FR network constitutes the entire NWM stream network while the MS resolution network is the FR network at or downstream of the AHPS forecast points shown. model but fails to consider backwater dynamics (Bedient et al., [2008;](#page-27-8) Gochis et al., [2021;](#page-28-8) Ponce & Changanti, [1994](#page-29-13)). The need for high resolution FIM at 10 m or better requires additional post-processing from the principal output of the NWM which is forecast river discharges at the reach scale. The use of a 2-dimensional (2D) hydrodynamic model across a continental-scale and high spatial resolutions is very cost prohibitive especially in an operational setting. The Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) terrain model is one such technique that can be used, along with synthetic rating curves (SRC), to convert 1-dimensional (1D) riverine discharges to stages, and finally to inundation extents.

### **1.3. HAND**

Nobre et al. ([2016\)](#page-29-14) showed evidence for utilizing the drainage normalizing HAND data set as a proxy for flood potential to make static flood inundation maps from known stages. The terrain index also provides additional utility in the observation of riverine flood inundation mapping from remote sensing especially in areas of high electromagnetic interference such as vegetated and anthropogenic areas (Aristizabal et al., [2020](#page-27-9); Aristizabal & Judge, [2021;](#page-27-10) Huang et al., [2017;](#page-28-9) Shastry et al., [2019;](#page-30-6) Twele et al., [2016](#page-30-7)). Zheng, Tarboton, et al. [\(2018](#page-30-8)) developed a methodology for determining stage-discharge relationships known as SRCs by sampling reach-averaged parameters from HAND data sets and inputting into the Manning's equation (Gauckler, [1867;](#page-28-10) Manning et al., [1890](#page-28-11)). This collection of methods, coupling HAND with SRCs, have been experimented with and compared to other sources of FIM

including engineering scale models, in-situ observation, and remote sensing based observation with solid results in large spatial scale applications (Afshari et al., [2018](#page-27-11); Godbout et al., [2019;](#page-28-12) Garousi-Nejad et al., [2019](#page-28-13); Hocini et al., [2020](#page-28-14); Johnson et al., [2019;](#page-28-15) Nobre et al., [2016](#page-29-14); Teng et al., [2015,](#page-30-9) [2017](#page-30-10); J. Zhang et al., [2018](#page-30-11); Zheng, Maidment, et al., [2018](#page-30-12)).

#### **1.4. HAND's Assumptions and Limitations**

HAND operates on many underlying assumptions since it can only be used as an inundation proxy or no physics model and thus, not a true hydrodynamic inundation model (Nobre et al., [2016;](#page-29-14) Y. Y. Liu et al., [2016;](#page-28-16) Y. Liu et al., [2020\)](#page-28-17). HAND, to our knowledge, has only been applied to natural, inland, and riverine inundation applications thus it is also missing pluvial, coastal, ground water, and dam break components among other possible sources of flooding. Additionally, in order to flood an area, HAND assumes all areas eligible for inundation must drain to some nearest flowpath which is used for catchment allocation and relative elevation calculation (Garousi-Nejad et al., [2019;](#page-28-13) Hocini et al., [2020](#page-28-14); Johnson et al., [2019;](#page-28-15) Y. Y. Liu et al., [2016](#page-28-16); Y. Liu et al., [2020;](#page-28-17) Maidment, [2017;](#page-28-18) Nobre et al., [2011](#page-29-15), [2016;](#page-29-14) Rennó et al., [2008](#page-29-16); Zheng, Maidment, et al., [2018](#page-30-12); Zheng, Tarboton, et al., [2018](#page-30-8)). Stream thalweg networks must also collectively drain to a singular outlet point for a given processing region (Nobre et al., [2016;](#page-29-14) Rennó et al., [2008](#page-29-16); Zheng, Maidment, et al., [2018\)](#page-30-12). Since elevations don't naturally do this, they must undergo a long series of hydro-conditioning processes to enforce monotonically decreasing elevations across an entire processing unit along with hydrologically correct directions of flow (Donchyts et al., [2016;](#page-27-12) Nobre et al., [2011](#page-29-15), [2016;](#page-29-14) Rennó et al., [2008](#page-29-16); Y. Y. Liu et al., [2016](#page-28-16); Y. Liu et al., [2020](#page-28-17)). The level of digital elevation map (DEM) manipulation required to enforce this assumption can be substantial depending on the region and can be a significant source of error. The drainage enforcing assumption also interacts with an inability to properly account for fluvial inundation in regions of DEM depressions that lack natural drainage to riverine areas (Nobre et al., [2016;](#page-29-14) Rennó et al., [2008](#page-29-16)).

When used for FIM applications, HAND assumes only fluvial inundation sourced from its nearest flowpath is accounted for (McGehee et al., [2016;](#page-29-17) Nobre et al., [2016](#page-29-14)). Catchments are independent of one another for FIM purposes meaning a reaches' stage value is only used to threshold the HAND values within its respective catchment (Y. Y. Liu et al., [2016;](#page-28-16) Zheng, Maidment, et al., [2018;](#page-30-12) Zheng, Tarboton, et al., [2018\)](#page-30-8). This assumption plays to the "Nearest Drainage" term in HAND and creates a significant limitation within HAND for FIM applications

ARISTIZABAL ET AL. 3 of 31

(Li et al., [2020;](#page-28-19) McGehee et al., [2016;](#page-29-17) Nobre et al., [2016](#page-29-14); J. Zhang et al., [2018](#page-30-11)). At the junction of high stream order and high flow rivers with lower flow tributaries, there can be a lack of inundation extents exhibited which is known colloquially in the forecasting community as the "catchment boundary problem." The academic community has somewhat referenced this issue before but it has been characterized more as a problem with the stream delineation process that comes from thresholding the drainage accumulation maps (Li et al., [2020](#page-28-19); Nobre et al., [2016\)](#page-29-14). Later in this study, we will re-introduce this problem and demonstrate how we initialize with a stream network (that of the NWM's) and thus avoid having to threshold accumulations to some arbitrary value to define stream networks. We illustrate how computing HAND independently for flowpaths of unit stream order can significantly enhance FIM performance by accounting for multiple sources of fluvial inundation that may exist in certain regions and flow scenarios.

### **1.5. HAND Implementations**

Due to significant advances in high performance computing (HPC) and large scale high resolution DEMs such as the 3D Elevation Program (3DEP) seamless at the 1/3 arc-sec (approximately 10 m depending on latitude) scale, HAND has been implemented into software for large-scale, continental computation. As part of the OWP's Innovators Program and NWC's Summer Institute, the National Flood Interoperability Experiment (NFIE) generated FIM hydrofabric (will be used interchangeably with the datasets produced by HAND) rapidly on a HPC (Maidment, [2017](#page-28-18); Y. Y. Liu et al., [2016](#page-28-16)). NFIE used open-source dependencies including the Terrain Analysis Using Digital Elevation Models (TauDEM) (Tarboton, [2005\)](#page-30-13) and the Geospatial Data Abstraction Library (GDAL) (Warmerdam, [2008\)](#page-30-14) to compute HAND for the Continental United States (CONUS) at 331 Hydrologic Unit Code (HUC) 6 processing units in 1.34 central processing unit (CPU) years. By allocating 31 nodes at 20 cores per node for a total of 620 available cores to the overall operation, it enabled the production to finish up in 36 hr consuming 3.2 terrabyte (TB) of peak memory and 5 TB of total disk space. Originally, NFIE utilized the NHD Medium Resolution (MR) to enforce flowpaths prior to further conditioning but more recent work has advanced this to the more current NHDPlus High Resolution (NHDPlusHR) which better agrees with the 10 m DEM from the NHDPlusHR program (Y. Liu et al., [2020\)](#page-28-17). The original NFIE data set was employed by the NWC as an unofficial demonstration to produce forecast FIM from the NWM for additional guidance in hydro-blind regions. Further work by Djokic ([2019\)](#page-27-13), implemented a series of improvements to HAND including equidistant reaches, updates to use with NHDPlusHR hydrography, and AGREE DEM reconditioning (Hellweger & Maidment, [1997\)](#page-28-20) into an ESRI Arc-Hydro workflow with use in ArcGIS. More notably the software added the ability to derive HAND on both the NWM FR and MS stream networks to consider multiple sources of fluvial inundation along high impact rivers of primary forecasting concern.

Related to these efforts, the United States Geological Survey (USGS) has invested in relative elevation HANDlike methods via work in the GIS Flood Tool (GFT) that also uses SRCs with cross-sections for stage-discharge relationships (Verdin et al., [2016](#page-30-15)). Additional investment by Petrochenkov [\(2020](#page-29-18)) was able to successfully scale this approach by transitioning the method to open-source Python source code (PyGFT) and implementing novel interpolation methods to help address some of the catchment boundary discontinuities discussed more in this paper. In addition to the domestic work done in the US, some studies have expanded upon HAND to cover global domains at 30 m resolutions (Donchyts et al., [2016](#page-27-12); Yamazaki et al., [2019\)](#page-30-16).
